newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU looks set to appeal WTO meat hormone ruling.
newsitem.headline: EU looks set to appeal WTO meat hormone ruling.

text.p: The European Commission seemed certain on Tuesday to appeal against a World Trade Organisation (WTO) dispute panel ruling that its ban on imports of hormone-treated meat breaks free trade rules.

"They (the WTO panel) have ruled that no member...is allowed to establish its own level of protection. Our view is contrary to that," a Commission spokesman told a news briefing. "It's quite clear that there will be an appeal."
The Commission said in a statement the panel failed to take properly into account scientific evidence presented by the EU in suport of its ban.
"The Commission considers that the matter must be brought before the appellate body of the WTO," it added.
Commission officials said a formal decision to appeal could only be taken after EU member states had been consulted.
Trade sources in Geneva said the ruling was delivered to EU and U.S. missions in Geneva on Monday.

Washington had been backed in its complaint by Australia, New Zealand, Canada and Norway. Argentina, which exports beef untreated with hormones to many EU member states, voiced support for the EU position.
An appeal would postpone for several more months any need for Brussels to take action to lift the 11-year-old ban.

EU officials have indicated they see little prospect of lifting the restrictions, officially imposed for health reasons, because of strong consumer pressure against the sale of beef treated with hormones.

If the EU loses an appeal -- as is almost certain -- but still declines to act, the WTO's Dispute Settlement Body (DSB) could ask the EU to pay compensation to the United States for the amount of trade it says it has lost.
If the EU were to refuse, the DSB -- on which all 131 WTO members have a voice -- could authorise U.S. trade retaliation to the same amount.

In 1989, two years after first bringing the case to the old General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT), the United States slapped 10 percent duties on a range of EU agricultural goods worth around $90 million a year.

In July last year, the EU asked the DSB to set up a panel to look into the legality of the U.S. counter-action but two weeks later Washington lifted the duties pending a decision in its case against Brussels.
When the initial ruling by the panel was sent to Brussels and Washington in May, the United States hailed the finding as backing its argument that the EU ban had no scientific basis.

U.S. Agriculture Department officials said at the time they wanted to see the EU market opened and were not especially interested in compensation. The U.S. beef industry says the ban has reduced sales to EU countries by at least $100 million a year and as much as $250 million.
